before.statement: **Statement refuted.** "If two complementary closed oriented submanifolds of a closed oriented manifold meet in exactly two points with opposite signs, then the pair can be removed by a Whitney move." **Counterexample.** On $T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ let $A=S^1\times\{0\}$ and let $B$ be the graph of a smooth circle map $f$ of degree $0$ with exactly two transverse crossings of $A$, both crossing $A$ with opposite signs (for instance $f(\theta)=\tfrac12\sin(2\pi\theta)$). Then $A\cap B=\{p,q\}$, $\varepsilon(p)=-\varepsilon(q)$, and $I(A,B)=0$; nevertheless the Whitney circle formed by half of $A$ and half of $B$ represents the nonzero class $(1,0)\in\pi_1(T^2)=\mathbb Z^2$, and for every admissible choice of arcs the class of the Whitney circle has the form $(j+1,0)\ne0$, because loops in $B$ are null-homotopic in $T^2$ while loops in $A$ change the first coordinate only. Hence no choice of arcs makes the circle null-homotopic, the group labels of $p$ and $q$ differ, and the Whitney trick cannot be applied even though the integer intersection number vanishes. This is exactly the extra obstruction in the non-simply-connected case.
before.strategy: 1.1 The graph $B$ of $f(\theta)=\tfrac12\sin(2\pi\theta)$ is an embedded circle, null-homotopic in $T^2$ (the map $f$ has degree $0$), crossing $A$ transversely at $\theta=0$ and $\theta=1/2$, where $f'(0)>0>f'(1/2)$; so the two local signs are opposite and $I(A,B)=0$ ([[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]], [[def-oriented-intersection-number]]). 1.2 Arc class: the arc in $B$ between $q$ and $p$ is a null-homotopic path in $T^2$ since $f$ has degree zero, while the arc in $A$ from $p$ to $q$ has first-coordinate displacement $1/2$, so the closed curve $\gamma=\alpha*\beta$ represents $(1,0)\ne0\in\pi_1(T^2)$ ([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]], [[def-whitney-circle-for-a-pair-of-intersection-points]]). 1.3 Arc independence: replacing $\alpha$ by another admissible arc changes $[\gamma]$ by the class of a loop in $A$ through $p$, i.e. by an element of $\langle(1,0)\rangle$, and loops in $B$ contribute $0$; hence the class of $\gamma$ is always of the form $(j+1,0)$ and is never trivial ([[lem-arcs-in-a-connected-submanifold-avoiding-finitely-many-double-points]], [[lem-fundamental-group-label-is-the-obstruction-to-contracting-the-whitney-circle]]). 1.4 Consequently the group labels differ, the group-ring condition $I(p)=-I(q)$ fails even though its augmentation $I(A,B)=0$ holds, and no Whitney disk exists for any admissible arc system; the mod-two count is even and the oriented count is zero, so neither detects the obstruction. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

after.statement: **Statement refuted.** "Two closed connected oriented complementary submanifolds meeting in exactly two opposite-sign points always admit a Whitney move cancelling the pair." **Counterexample.** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth approximation and tubular-neighbourhood suppliers used below. There are embedded oriented spheres $A,B\cong S^3$ in the closed oriented manifold $X=(S^3\times S^3)\#(S^1\times S^5)$ with $\pi_1(X)=\langle t\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, such that $A\cap B=\{p,q\}$ transversely with signs $+1,-1$, while every admissible Whitney circle for the ordered pair $(p,q)$ represents $t\ne1$ (after fixing the generator convention). Construct $A=S^3\times\{y_0\}$ in the product summand. Take two parallel spheres $C_i=\{x_i\}\times S^3$, give $C_1$ its product orientation and $C_2$ the opposite orientation, and join them away from $A$ by an oriented tube whose core winds once through the $S^1\times S^5$ summand. The connected sum $B=C_1\#(-C_2)$ is an embedded $S^3$. Its only intersections with $A$ are $p=(x_1,y_0)$ and $q=(x_2,y_0)$. With whiskers normalized at $p$, their group labels are $1,t$, so their equivariant indices are $1,-t$ in $\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$. The integer intersection is $1-1=0$, but no Whitney circle bounds even a continuous disk. Both sheets are simply connected, so their inclusions are $\pi_1$-trivial and the group labels are well-defined independently of paths in the sheets. Thus opposite signs and vanishing integer intersection do not supply the Whitney move in a nonsimply-connected ambient manifold.
after.strategy:
**Given:** The product $S^3\times S^3$, distinct nearby $x_1,x_2$ in its first factor, $y_0$ in its second factor, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the cited smooth suppliers.

1.1 Form $X$ by removing a small $6$-ball disjoint from $A=S^3\times\{y_0\}$ and $C_1\cup C_2$ in the product, removing a ball from $S^1\times S^5$, and identifying their boundary $5$-spheres by an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism. This explicitly defines the smooth oriented connected sum. Removing either ball does not change the fundamental group: apply van Kampen to the punctured manifold and the ball, with collar overlap homotopy equivalent to the simply connected $S^5$. The same theorem across the neck gives $\pi_1(X)=1*\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Here $S^3,S^5$ are simply connected. The fundamental-group-of-a-product theorem gives $\pi_1(S^1\times S^5)=\pi_1(S^1)\times\pi_1(S^5)=\mathbb Z\times1$, using the circle theorem; projection to $S^1$ induces the stated isomorphism. Choose its generator orientation below. [given, construct]

1.2 Choose small $3$-balls $D_i\subset C_i$ away from $A$ and paths in $C_i$ from their centres $u_i$ to $p$ or $q$, respectively. Fix an embedded arc $\alpha$ in $A$ from $p$ to $q$. A reference arc from $u_2$ to $u_1$ in the product, otherwise missing $A,C_1,C_2$, can be chosen in product coordinates; the loop obtained by adjoining the fixed sheet paths and $\alpha$ is null-homotopic since the product is simply connected. Replace a short segment of this reference arc by a detour through the connected-sum neck, around one generator of the $S^1$ factor, and back through the neck. Two parallel lanes make the outward and return portions disjoint. More formally, relative endpoint smoothing followed by the compact-arc embedding supplier gives an embedded representative of this path class; make its interior transverse to each of the three $3$-dimensional sheets, keeping short fixed endpoint collars normal to $C_i$. Since $1+3-6=-2$, its interior misses every sheet. Finitely many compactly supported perturbations suffice and preserve its relative path class and embeddedness. Denote the resulting embedded core arc by $\eta:u_2\to u_1$. By the construction, closing $\eta$ using the fixed sheet paths and $\alpha$ gives the generator $t$, not a null loop. [construct, step 1.1]

1.3 A sufficiently thin tubular neighbourhood of $\eta$ is $I\times D^5$: its normal bundle is trivial because the base is an interval. Choose a rank-$3$ subbundle in that normal bundle agreeing with the tangent $3$-planes of $C_i$ at its endpoints. Such a choice exists because the space of $3$-planes in $\mathbb R^5$ is path-connected; endpoint frames can be joined and interpolated on the interval. The resulting $I\times D^3$ has end balls $D_i$ after shrinking and straightening in endpoint charts. Remove their interiors from $C_1\cup C_2$ and insert the lateral cylinder $I\times S^2$, rounding its corners. Use the gluing that extends the specified orientations $C_1,-C_2$; an endpoint reflection realizes the required orientation convention. The tube and all rounding lie away from $A$ and the rest of the sheets. Each punctured $C_i$ is a $3$-ball, and two such balls joined by $S^2\times I$ form $S^3$. Thus the result is an embedded oriented sphere $B$; it agrees with $C_1$ near $p$ and with $-C_2$ near $q$. Their product tangent spaces are complementary to $TA$, so the only intersections are $p,q$ with signs $+1,-1$. [construct, step 1.2]

1.4 Take an embedded arc $\beta$ in $B$ from $q$ to $p$ running through the tube. Its part in the tube is homotopic relative endpoints to its core $\eta$ inside the tubular neighbourhood; its end parts are the fixed sheet paths up to homotopy in the punctured spheres. Consequently $[\alpha*\beta]=t$ by step 1.2. Any other paths with the same endpoints in $A$ and $B$ are homotopic relative endpoints to these, since both sheets are $S^3$. In particular every admissible arc system gives the same nontrivial class. Normalize the label at $p$ to $1$; the label comparison lemma then gives the other label $t$, up to replacing the generator by its inverse under the opposite convention. The indices $1,-t$ are not negatives of each other, although their augmentation is zero. A disk filling a Whitney circle would contract $t$, impossible. Hence no Whitney disk or Whitney move exists for this pair. [step 1.1, step 1.3, step 1.2, construct] ∎

before.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. On the torus $T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ let $A=S^1\times\{0\}$ and let $B\subseteq T^2$ be the graph of a smooth degree-zero circle map chosen to meet $A$ transversely in exactly four points whose local oriented signs are $+,+,+,-$. Then $I_2(A,B)=0$ while $I(A,B)=2\ne0$. Consequently no homotopy, hence no isotopy, of $A$ can make $A$ disjoint from $B$, even though both the mod-two count and the parity of the number of intersection points are trivial; in particular parity provides pairs of points but neither opposite oriented signs, nor null-homotopy of the Whitney circles, nor extendibility of framings, so the hypotheses of the Whitney move cannot be read off from mod-two data. The same computation shows that the oriented intersection number, not the parity, is the cancellation-invariant of the two-sheet problem.
before.strategy: 1.1 Construction: let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth map with $g(\theta+1)=g(\theta)$ and $\int_0^1g'=0$ (degree zero), chosen so that $g^{-1}(\mathbb Z)=\{\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3,\theta_4\}$ are transverse crossings with signs $+,+,+,-$ (a small bump perturbation of the constant map gives one $+$ and one $-$ crossing, repeated for a second pair; the exact values are checked in the proof). Let $B$ be the image of $\theta\mapsto(\theta,g(\theta))$ in $T^2$ and $A=S^1\times\{0\}$. 1.2 Signs and counts: at each crossing the local sign is the sign of $g'(\theta_i)$ ([[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]], [[def-oriented-intersection-number]]), so $I(A,B)=1+1+1-1=2$, while the number of points is $4$ and $I_2(A,B)=4\equiv0$ ([[def-mod-two-intersection-number]], [[cor-oriented-intersection-reduces-to-mod-two-intersection]]). 1.3 Invariance: $I(A,\cdot)$ is a homotopy invariant and changes sign under factor interchange ([[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]], [[thm-intersection-number-under-factor-interchange]]); a disjoint pair has intersection number $0$, so no homotopy of $A$ can produce a disjoint configuration. 1.4 Conclusion: the vanishing of the mod-two count therefore carries no information about the oriented pairing, and the Whitney move, whose first hypothesis is the oriented condition $\varepsilon(p)=-\varepsilon(q)$ for a cancelling pair followed by the group-label and framing conditions, cannot be driven by parity. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

after.statement: On the oriented torus $T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$, orient $A=S^1\times\{0\}$ and $B=\{(\theta,2\theta):\theta\in S^1\}$ by increasing $\theta$. Then $A\cap B$ consists of exactly two transverse points, each of local oriented sign $+1$. Thus $I_2(A,B)=0$ but $I(A,B)=2\ne0$. Homotopy invariance of oriented intersection implies that no homotopy, hence no isotopy, of $A$ can make it disjoint from $B$. In particular even parity alone does not supply a Whitney move: the only pair already fails the necessary opposite-sign condition. This example establishes that mod-two vanishing does not imply oriented cancellability; it makes no separate claim about the independence of the label and framing conditions.
after.strategy:
**Given:** $T^2$ with orientation $d\theta\wedge dy$, $A(\theta)=(\theta,0)$, and $B(\theta)=(\theta,2\theta\bmod1)$, both oriented by increasing parameter.

1.1 The first coordinate makes $B$ an embedded circle. Its intersections with $A$ are exactly $\theta=0,1/2$. The ordered tangent pair $((1,0),(1,2))$ has determinant $2>0$ at each intersection, so both signs are $+1$. Hence $I(A,B)=2$ and $I_2(A,B)=2\bmod2=0$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 If a homotopy of $A$ ended at a map disjoint from $B$, its endpoint intersection number would be zero, contrary to homotopy invariance of the initial value $2$. An isotopy is such a homotopy. A Whitney move cancels a pair of opposite local signs, and these two signs are equal. Therefore mod-two evenness supplies no Whitney cancellation in this example. [step 1.1] ∎

before.strategy: 1.1 The case with $r\ge3$ reduces to the stable-range theorem with the roles of the two sheets arranged so that the small-dimensional sheet is the one treated by the immersion argument; the new content is the case $r=2$ (and $r=1$, excluded here by $r+s\ge5$ and the complementary-dimension bookkeeping). 1.2 For $r=2$ the null-homotopy disk cannot be embedded by dimension count ($2+r-m=0$ for $s=m-2$), so one works instead with an immersion: trivialize the normal bundle of the disk (it is contractible), push the disk off $A$, and use the hypothesis on $\pi_1(X\setminus B)$ to make the complement's fundamental group control the remaining intersections; this is the source's reduction. 1.3 The framing of the Whitney circle is then constructed by the parallel-translation argument with the tangency conditions along the two arcs, exactly as in the stable case. 1.4 The final isotopy is the transported plane model as before. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

after.strategy:
**Given:** The oriented sheets, opposite-sign points, specified null-homotopic arc loop, $s\ge3$, $m=r+s\ge5$, and the additional injection $\pi_1(X\setminus B)\to\pi_1(X)$ when $r\le2$.

1.1 The stable case is $r\ge3$. The remaining cases are $r=1$ and $r=2$; $r=1$ forces $s\ge4$ and is permitted. A generic disk has expected intersection dimension $2+s-m=2-r$ with $B$, so ordinary general position alone does not clear $B$ in these two cases. First construct Milnor's boundary annulus around the prescribed loop using opposite intersection signs and the oriented normal to $B$. Its inner boundary lies in $X\setminus(A\cup B)$ and is null-homotopic in $X$. For $r\ge3$, codimension $r$ of $B$ makes it contractible in $X\setminus B$; for $r=1,2$, the assumed injection gives precisely the same conclusion. [given, construct]

1.2 Inside $X\setminus B$, clear $A$ from a null-homotopy using its codimension $s\ge3$: the expected intersection dimension is $2+r-m=2-s\le-1$. Thus the shifted boundary circle contracts in $X\setminus(A\cup B)$. Relative smoothing and the $m\ge5$ disk-embedding theorem provide an embedded disk there, agreeing with the annulus near its boundary. This is Milnor's clean embedded disk construction; a disk normal trivialization alone would not remove sheet intersections. [given, step 1.1, construct]

1.3 Extend the model to its normal directions using Milnor's Lemma 6.13 frame construction. The required Stiefel space for the $(r-1)$-frame is simply connected because $s\ge3$, and the remaining oriented normal frame extends over the contractible disk. When $r=1$, the $(r-1)$-frame is empty; the normal line choice along the $B$ arc matches at both endpoints because the two intersection signs are opposite. There is no omitted $r=1$ case. [given, step 1.2, construct]

1.4 Transport the plane-model isotopy through this product embedding and extend it by the identity outside its neighbourhood. It removes precisely $p,q$ and fixes a neighbourhood of the other intersection points, as in Milnor's Theorem 6.6. [step 1.3, construct] ∎

before.statement: **Statement refuted.** "If $X^4$ is a smooth $4$-manifold and $W:D^2\looparrowright X$ is a smoothly immersed disk whose boundary is an embedded circle $\gamma$, then $W$ can be homotoped relative to its boundary to an embedded disk; in particular the interior double points of an immersed Whitney disk can be ignored." **Counterexample.** Let $X=B^4$ and let $\gamma=K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$ be a trefoil knot. The cone on $K$ is a continuous disk in $B^4$ that is smooth away from the cone point; a small perturbation of the model makes it a smooth immersion with a single transverse interior double point and boundary $K$. No smoothly embedded disk in $B^4$ has boundary $K$: a smoothly slice knot has Alexander polynomial of the form $A(t)=p(t)p(1/t)$ (Fox-Milnor), while the trefoil has $A(t)=t^2-t+1$ up to units and $A(-1)=3$ is not a square. Hence the immersed disk cannot be cleaned, interior double points are genuinely non-removable in dimension four, and the general-position step of the stable range ($a,b\le m-3=1$ fails for $a=b=2$) cannot be replaced by an immersion argument. This is the concrete shape of the failure of the smooth Whitney trick in dimension four.
before.strategy: 1.1 The trefoil $K\subset S^3$ bounds a continuous disk in $B^4$ (the cone over $K$) that is smooth on $B^4\setminus\{0\}$; smoothing the cone point and perturbing gives a smooth immersion $W:D^2\looparrowright B^4$ with boundary $K$ and one transverse interior double point ([[cor-every-continuous-map-between-smooth-manifolds-is-homotopic-to-a-smooth-map]]); thus an immersed disk with boundary $K$ exists, so it is a candidate for an immersed Whitney disk ([[def-whitney-disk-and-clean-framed-whitney-disk]]). 1.2 Non-existence of an embedded disk: if a smoothly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ had $\partial D=K$, then $K$ would be smoothly slice; by the Fox-Milnor condition (cited in the references of this item) a smoothly slice knot has $A(t)=p(t)p(1/t)$ up to units, so $|A(-1)|$ is a square. 1.3 Computation: the trefoil's Alexander polynomial is $A(t)=t^2-t+1$ up to units, giving $A(-1)=3$, not a square; hence the trefoil is not slice and no embedded disk with boundary $K$ exists. 1.4 Therefore the immersed disk cannot be homotoped rel boundary to an embedded disk; since $m=4$ and $a=b=2$ violate $a,b\le m-3=1$, the clean-disk lemma of the stable range does not apply, and the interior double point cannot be removed by the methods of this page: this is exactly the failure recorded in the dimension-four remark. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

after.statement: **Statement refuted.** "Every smooth properly immersed disk in $B^4$ with embedded boundary can be homotoped relative to the boundary to a smooth properly embedded disk." **Counterexample.** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the local smooth nonsliceness suppliers. The trefoil $K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$ bounds a smooth properly immersed disk with exactly one transverse interior double point. Use the trefoil diagram given by the closure of the two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$. Changing its middle crossing gives $\sigma_1\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_1$, whose closure is the unknot after a Reidemeister-II cancellation and a Reidemeister-I move. The trace of this single crossing change in a collar $S^3\times[0,\varepsilon]\subset B^4$ is an immersed annulus with exactly one transverse double point. Cap its inner unknot boundary by an embedded disk deeper in $B^4$ and smooth the join. No smooth properly embedded disk with boundary $K$ exists: the locally proved branched-cover nonsliceness lemma excludes it. The boundary cover has first homology of order $3$, whereas a slice-disk cover would be a rational homology ball whose boundary first homology has square order. Hence this immersed disk cannot be cleaned relative to its boundary. It witnesses the failure of unrestricted disk cleaning in smooth dimension four; by itself it does not specify two transverse sheets making $K$ a Whitney circle or supply the boundary framing data of a Whitney disk.
after.strategy:
**Given:** The trefoil $K$ as the closure of $\sigma_1^3$ and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1.1 Change the middle positive crossing to a negative crossing. The braid word becomes $\sigma_1\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_1$; cancel the inverse adjacent crossings by a Reidemeister-II isotopy. The closure of the remaining one-crossing two-strand braid is an unknot (remove its kink by Reidemeister I). Thus there is a knot movie from $K$ to the unknot containing exactly one crossing change, all other stages being isotopies. [given, construct]

1.2 Put this movie into $S^3\times[0,\varepsilon]$ by sending a strand point at movie time $t$ to $(k_t(u),t)$. Away from the crossing-change time, each time slice is embedded and the time coordinate separates distinct slices. Near the event use spatial coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and time $t$, with the two sheets parametrized by $(u,t)\mapsto(u,0,t,t)$ and $(v,t)\mapsto(0,v,-t,t)$. They coincide only at $u=v=t=0$. Their tangent planes are spanned by $(1,0,0,0),(0,0,1,1)$ and by $(0,1,0,0),(0,0,-1,1)$, respectively; these four vectors are independent. Both branches are immersions and meet transversely at this single point. Patch this local movie to the stationary outside strands, and choose stationary time collars at both endpoints. This constructs an immersed annulus with exactly one transverse interior double point. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.3 The unknot at the inner collar level bounds an embedded disk in the remaining inner ball: carry a standard disk by an ambient isotopy identifying that unknot with a standard round circle, and push its interior inward. This disk lies outside the open movie collar. Glue it to the annulus and round the corner using their stationary collars; no new intersections arise. Annulus plus disk is a disk, and its outer collar meets $\partial B^4$ transversely in $K$. Therefore the resulting proper immersion has exactly the one double point of step 1.2. [step 1.2, construct]

1.4 The local trefoil nonsliceness lemma proves that no smooth proper embedded disk has boundary $K$: a putative slice disk would have a rationally acyclic branched double cover, but its trefoil boundary cover has first homology of order $3$, contradicting the locally proved square-order consequence of duality. Thus the immersed disk cannot be homotoped relative to its boundary to a proper embedding. This is a disk-cleaning obstruction; calling the disk a Whitney disk additionally requires sheet arcs and their boundary data, which are not part of this witness. [given, step 1.3] ∎

new_items.title: The double cover branched over a slice disk is a rational homology ball
new_items.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $D\subset B^4$ is a smooth proper embedded disk, the connected double cover $W\to B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented smooth $4$-manifold with $H_i(W;\mathbb F_2)=0$ for $i>0$, hence $H_i(W;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $i>0$. Its boundary is the double cover of $S^3$ branched over $\partial D$.
new_items.strategy:
**Given:** A proper smooth disk $D$ and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for tubular, smooth and CW suppliers.

1.1 The oriented rank-two normal bundle of $D$ is trivial, so its closed tubular neighbourhood is $N=D\times D^2$, with boundary-compatible charts near $\partial D$. Let $Y$ be the closure of the complement of its interior, with the corners rounded. A collar-thickened Mayer–Vietoris cover of $B^4=N\cup Y$ has overlap homotopy equivalent to $D\times S^1$. Since $B^4,N,D$ are contractible, Mayer–Vietoris shows that $Y$ is connected, its positive homology is zero except $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$, and inclusion of a normal meridian circle induces the isomorphism in degree one. The boundary complement has the same meridian generator under inclusion. Reduction modulo two gives a surjective homomorphism $\pi_1(Y)\to\mathbb Z/2$ by abelianization. The usual path-class construction gives its connected double cover $\widetilde Y$: paths starting at a base point are identified when their endpoints agree and their concatenation has even meridian class; small simply connected coordinate balls provide its covering charts. [given, construct]

1.2 Over $\mathbb F_2$ there is a short exact sequence of singular chain complexes $0\to C_*(Y)\xrightarrow{T}C_*(\widetilde Y)\xrightarrow{P}C_*(Y)\to0$. Define $T$ of a singular simplex as the sum of its two lifts; define $P$ by projection. Every simplex lifts because its domain is contractible; the two lifts are exchanged by the deck transformation. Boundary commutes with both maps, and in each free pair of lifted simplices the kernel of projection is exactly their sum. Thus the sequence is exact without an equivariant triangulation. Connectedness makes $P:H_0(\widetilde Y)\to H_0(Y)$ an isomorphism and $T:H_0(Y)\to H_0(\widetilde Y)$ zero. The connecting map $H_1(Y)\to H_0(Y)$ is therefore an isomorphism, by exactness and the one-dimensionality of both groups. The same sequence yields $H_i(\widetilde Y)=0$ for $i>1$ and $T:H_1(Y)\to H_1(\widetilde Y)$ an isomorphism. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.3 The preimage of $D\times S^1$ is the connected fiberwise double cover $D\times S^1$, because its meridian has odd class. Naturality of the chain sequence with respect to inclusion of this meridian circle shows that its lifted circle maps isomorphically onto $H_1(\widetilde Y;\mathbb F_2)$: transfer on $H_1$ is an isomorphism for both the circle cover and the cover of $Y$, and the bottom inclusion is an isomorphism. Glue a new copy of $D\times D^2$ to $\widetilde Y$ along this overlap, using $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z^2)$ as the covering map into the original tubular neighbourhood. This gives a smooth branched cover: outside the disk it is a covering map and near the disk these are complex normal coordinates. It is compact, connected and oriented, and its boundary has the asserted branched-cover description. Mayer–Vietoris now gives $H_i(W;\mathbb F_2)=0$ for all $i>0$, since the overlap's $H_1$ maps isomorphically onto that of $\widetilde Y$ and all higher groups of both pieces vanish. [step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

1.4 The double of $W$ is a compact smooth manifold without boundary. Its CW homotopy model has compact image for the forward equivalence, hence that image lies in a finite subcomplex; composing the reverse equivalence with the folding retraction from the double onto $W$ shows that $W$ is homotopy dominated by a finite CW complex. Therefore each integral homology group of $W$ is finitely generated. The homology universal coefficient sequence over $\mathbb F_2$ injects $H_i(W;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb F_2$ into $H_i(W;\mathbb F_2)$; its vanishing in positive degrees implies that each such integral homology group has rank zero. Tensoring with $\mathbb Q$ proves rational acyclicity. [step 1.3, construct, algebra] ∎

new_items.title: A rational homology four-ball has square boundary torsion order
new_items.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented smooth $4$-manifold with connected boundary $M$ and the rational homology of a point. Then $M$ is a rational homology $3$-sphere and $|H_1(M;\mathbb Z)|$ is a square.
new_items.strategy:
**Given:** Such $W,M$; all homology groups below have integral coefficients unless a coefficient field is written.

1.1 Homology groups of a compact smooth manifold with boundary are finitely generated: double the manifold, use its CW homotopy model, place the compact image of the equivalence in a finite subcomplex, and fold back, obtaining finite CW domination. Rational Poincaré–Lefschetz duality and the long exact sequence show that the connected boundary $M$ is a rational homology sphere. Integral duality on $M$ gives $H_2(M)=H^1(M)=0$ because $H_1(M)$ is finite. The relative fundamental class maps to the boundary fundamental class, so $H_4(W,M)\to H_3(M)$ is an isomorphism. Also $H_3(W,M)=H^1(W)=0$, by the cohomology universal coefficient sequence and finite $H_1(W)$. Exactness then gives $H_3(W)=0$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Put $A=H_2(W)$ and $B=H_1(W)$, both finite. Duality and the cohomology universal coefficient sequence give $H_2(W,M)\cong H^2(W)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(B,\mathbb Z)$ and $H_1(W,M)\cong H^3(W)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(A,\mathbb Z)$. For a finite abelian group $F$, its Ext group has order $|F|$: decompose into cyclic groups and apply $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$, which computes $\operatorname{Ext}(\mathbb Z/n,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/n$. The pair sequence, with $H_2(M)=0$ and $H_0(M)\to H_0(W)$ an isomorphism, is therefore $0\to A\to\operatorname{Ext}(B,\mathbb Z)\to H_1(M)\to B\to\operatorname{Ext}(A,\mathbb Z)\to0$. Multiplying orders in this exact sequence yields $|H_1(M)|=(|B|/|A|)^2$. The injection on the left ensures $|A|$ divides $|B|$, so this is the square of an integer. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

new_items.title: The trefoil does not bound a smooth proper disk in the four-ball
new_items.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The trefoil knot does not bound a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$.
new_items.strategy:
**Given:** The standard three-crossing trefoil, oriented meridians to its three diagram arcs, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1.1 Apply van Kampen to the diagram complement, split above and below the projection plane and use small crossing balls. The upper region has one meridian generator for each diagram arc; attaching each crossing ball identifies the outgoing under-meridian with the conjugate of the incoming under-meridian by the over-meridian, since sliding its based normal circle past the over-strand traverses that over-meridian and its inverse. Label the three arcs $a,b,c$ cyclically so that the relations are $c=aba^{-1}$, $a=bcb^{-1}$, $b=cac^{-1}$. These are the three positive crossings of the standard trefoil diagram. Substitute the first relation into the second to get $aba=bab$; the third then follows from these two. The knot exterior thus has group $G=\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$, with $a,b$ meridians and the abelianization taking each to $1\in\mathbb Z$. This supplies the particular diagram computation rather than importing a general Wirtinger theorem. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 The unbranched double cover of the exterior is the kernel $K$ of the mod-two meridian homomorphism $G\to\mathbb Z/2$, by the based-path construction of the cover. To extend it across the branch knot, glue the cover of its solid-torus neighbourhood by squaring each normal disk coordinate. The meridian upstairs then projects to the square of a meridian downstairs. Van Kampen kills its normal closure in $K$. Killing all such lifted meridians gives exactly the kernel of the parity map on $G/\langle\!\langle a^2,b^2\rangle\!\rangle$: the normal subgroup is generated by conjugates of meridian squares, and all those conjugates lie in $K$; both choices of lift are included when the boundary covering torus is filled. Thus the branched boundary cover has group equal to that kernel. [step 1.1, construct]

1.3 The quotient has presentation $\langle a,b\mid a^2=b^2=1,\ aba=bab\rangle$. With involutions the last relation is $(ab)^3=1$. Reducing words by $a^2=b^2=1$ and $(ab)^3=1$ leaves at most six possibilities, namely $1,ab,(ab)^2,a,(ab)a,(ab)^2a$. Sending $a,b$ to adjacent transpositions in the permutation group of three letters satisfies the relations and yields all six permutations, so the quotient has exactly six elements. Parity is their permutation sign; its kernel consists of the three powers of $ab$ and is cyclic of order three. Consequently the branched double cover $M$ has $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/3$, by abelianization of its fundamental group. [step 1.2, algebra]

1.4 If the trefoil bounded a smooth proper disk, the disk-cover lemma would give a compact oriented rational homology four-ball $W$ with boundary $M$. The square-order lemma would force $|H_1(M)|$ to be a square. Its value is $3$, contradiction. [step 1.3] ∎
